name: Pupillary light reflex pathway
summary: Light in either eye constricts both pupils because the pathway is bilateral at two points. Retinal ganglion cell axons leave the optic tract before the lateral geniculate body and reach the pretectal nuclei of both sides (via the brachium of the superior colliculus and the posterior commissure); each pretectal nucleus projects to both Edinger–Westphal nuclei; each Edinger–Westphal nucleus sends preganglionic fibers in the oculomotor nerve to the ciliary ganglion, whose postganglionic fibers reach the sphincter pupillae through the short ciliary nerves. Asymmetric afferent lesions produce the relative afferent pupillary defect, efferent lesions a fixed dilated pupil, and pretectal lesions light-near dissociation.

origin.note: Intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (melanopsin) and conventional ganglion cells.

neuronChain.synapse: Edinger–Westphal nuclei of both sides via the posterior commissure
sphincter pupillae via the short ciliary nerves

decussation.note: Bilateral at the chiasm and again between the pretectal and Edinger–Westphal nuclei, giving the consensual response.

waypoints.note: afferent limb in the optic nerve and tract
fibers leave the optic tract before the LGN via the brachium of the superior colliculus
preganglionic fibers on the surface of the nerve
short ciliary nerves to the sphincter pupillae (represented by the orbital region)

termination: Sphincter pupillae of both eyes (direct and consensual constriction).

lesionEffectsByLevel.effects: Relative afferent pupillary defect: the affected pupil dilates when the light swings onto it; both pupils are equal in size
Contralateral RAPD with a homonymous hemianopia
Light-near dissociation of both pupils (Parinaud, Argyll Robertson)
Fixed dilated pupil with ptosis and ophthalmoplegia

lesionEffectsByLevel.level: Ciliary ganglion or short ciliary nerves
lesionEffectsByLevel.effects: Adie tonic pupil: large, slow to near, supersensitive to dilute pilocarpine
Fixed dilated pupil that does not constrict to full-strength pilocarpine

pearls: Both pupils are always the same size in an afferent lesion; anisocoria means an efferent (or iris) problem
The swinging flashlight test is the only bedside test that can detect an asymmetric optic nerve lesion in a patient with good acuity
Light-near dissociation localizes to the pretectum or to the ciliary ganglion with aberrant regeneration
